title: Designing a Brand for a Real Estate Team
description: A behind-the-scenes look at the logo, typography, color palette, and visual identity I designed for a Brooklyn real estate team.
body:
What does it take to design a brand for a real estate team that wants to feel premium, distinctive, and unmistakably its own?

For The Savory Team, the process started with a lot of work that already existed—and a feeling that something still wasn't quite right.

In this article, I'll walk you through the real estate branding project: what the client brought to me, how I explored the identity, and why I made the design decisions behind the SAVORY wordmark.

This is a working draft for shaping the story and the video.

In this article

  1. The client and the challenge
  2. Starting with existing work
  3. Finding the right direction
  4. Exploring logo and monogram ideas
  5. Choosing the right typeface
  6. Creating a distinctive wordmark
  7. Giving the logo an idea
  8. Choosing the color palette
  9. Presenting the brand in context
  10. Building a usable identity

1. The client and the challenge

The Savory Team is a Brooklyn real estate team that wanted its brand to feel as considered as the experience it offers.

The direction needed to feel premium and sophisticated, but also artistic and connected to New York—not stiff or corporate.

The challenge was to create a distinct visual identity the team could use across its real estate marketing.

That meant thinking beyond the logo on its own: the identity had to work with property photography, social posts, email, and signage.

2. Starting with existing work

When the team contacted me, it had already spent months working on its branding with the Compass design team.

The team had a wordmark, a monogram, colors, typography, and plenty of ideas, but the identity still didn't feel quite finished.

Scott also used Perplexity to explore typefaces, colors, and applications before looking for a designer to help bring the brand together.

He initially described the project as being almost done and asked me to refine the existing direction.

As we explored the work together, that request grew into a new wordmark and a broader identity.

3. Finding the right direction

Before designing anything new, I wanted to understand what the client liked about the existing work and what still felt off.

We looked at the relationship between the SAVORY wordmark and the ST monogram, the typefaces, the colors, and the references the team had collected.

Some parts had the right character, while others didn't yet feel like they belonged to the same identity.

Rather than throwing everything away, I used that work as a starting point for the next round of exploration.

4. Exploring logo and monogram ideas

I explored a range of directions, from wordmarks and monograms to stamp-like marks and custom letterforms.

My Figma file got messy, and that's a normal part of the process.

Each option helped us understand the tradeoffs between elegance, personality, legibility, and how much detail the mark could carry.

Some connected-letter ideas felt too playful for the direction the client wanted.

Other versions felt clean but lost the character that made the starting point interesting.

The goal was not more options for the sake of options.

It was to find the right balance for this particular team.

5. Choosing the right typeface

For a wordmark-led identity, the typeface has to carry a lot of the brand's personality.

We looked for a serif with a sophisticated, editorial quality that could feel premium without becoming too formal or generic.

The team had already compared a number of fonts and paid attention to the character of individual letters.

During the project, we explored a reference that led me to Roxborough CF as a direction for the wordmark.

Its high contrast and expressive letterforms offered the presence I wanted for the name.

I set SAVORY in uppercase to give the wordmark a strong, confident appearance when it stood on its own.

For the wider identity, an italic editorial typeface provided a contrasting voice for longer phrases and supporting applications.

6. Creating a distinctive wordmark

A strong real estate brand doesn't necessarily need a literal house, key, or building in its logo.

Sometimes the name itself can become the most recognizable part of the identity.

With SAVORY, I wanted the wordmark to feel refined at first glance, while giving it one detail that made it its own.

That meant paying attention to the typeface, the spacing, and how the letters worked together—not simply choosing a font and typing the name.

7. Giving the logo an idea

The distinctive detail in this direction is the shifted O.

The two parts of the letter sit apart, giving an otherwise classic wordmark an unexpected point of interest.

The idea connects to finding your place: a visual movement that relates to the team's work helping people find a home.

It also creates a compact element that can be explored beyond the full wordmark.

We discussed whether the abstract shape might be read differently at first glance, so the relationship between the full name, the small mark, and motion was an important part of the design conversation.

8. Choosing the color palette

The color palette needed to support the same sophisticated but expressive character.

We explored variations of red, blue, and light neutrals as the identity developed.

The direction settled on a rich, wax-like red and an off-white pairing that gives the wordmark contrast and warmth.

For me, a premium look comes from how the type, color, and distinctive detail work together, not from a single color or a serif font alone.

The earlier blue combinations were explorations along the way, not the final palette decision.

9. Presenting the brand in context

I don't want a client to judge a logo only as black artwork on a white page.

I want them to see how it could appear where their audience actually encounters the brand.

For a real estate team, that includes property photography, social posts, a profile image, email, and signage.

These applications help reveal whether the wordmark has enough presence, whether the colors have enough contrast, and whether a secondary mark works at a small size.

They also help the team understand the identity as a connected system, rather than a collection of isolated logo options.

10. Building a usable identity

The work doesn't end with choosing a wordmark.

The team also needs the right logo variations, colors, typography, files, and guidelines to use the identity consistently.

For Savory, the project expanded to include a broader style guide, social templates, and an email signature with motion for the team and its brokerage handoff.

Those practical details are what help a visual idea move from a presentation into a system people can work with.

Conclusion: A brand is built through decisions

This project began with a client who already had a direction and wanted a few things to feel right.

Through exploration and feedback, it became an opportunity to create a new wordmark and develop a more complete visual identity.

The lesson is simple: an effective brand isn't just a font, a color, or a symbol.

It's the way those choices come together to express a business and work across its real applications.

Explore the Savory project, or get in touch if you need help designing an identity for your business.
